subject: pe
promptStrong: Give me a challenging GCSE exam-style question on components of fitness, principles of training and training methods, then mark my answer against the spec.
promptWeak: Explain components of fitness, principles of training and training methods for GCSE PE simply, with an example and the most common mistake.

questions.q: Which component of fitness is defined as the ability of the whole body to work for long periods, supplying oxygen and nutrients to the muscles?
questions.explain: Cardiovascular endurance (aerobic endurance) is the ability of the heart, lungs and blood to keep supplying oxygen for sustained whole-body exercise, e.g. long-distance running.

questions.q: Which component of fitness is best defined as strength multiplied by speed (the ability to do strength work quickly)?
questions.explain: Power (also called explosive strength) = strength x speed. Examples include a sprint start, a long jump take-off or a spike in volleyball.

questions.q: A netball player quickly changes direction to dodge an opponent. Which component of fitness is she mainly using?
questions.explain: Agility is the ability to change direction quickly while keeping control. Dodging and changing direction at speed is a classic use of agility.

questions.q: Which component of fitness is the time taken to respond to a stimulus?
questions.explain: Reaction time is how quickly a performer responds to a stimulus, such as a sprinter reacting to the starting gun.

questions.q: A gymnast holding a handstand steady is mainly demonstrating which component of fitness?
questions.explain: Balance is maintaining the centre of mass over the base of support. Holding a handstand is static balance.

questions.q: The Multi-Stage Fitness Test (bleep test) is used to measure which component of fitness?
questions.explain: The Multi-Stage Fitness Test estimates cardiovascular endurance (and VO2 max) as the runner completes 20m shuttles at an increasing pace.

questions.q: The sit and reach test measures which component of fitness?
questions.explain: The sit and reach test measures flexibility, particularly of the lower back and hamstrings.

questions.q: Which test would you use to measure explosive leg power?
questions.explain: The vertical jump (Sargent) test measures explosive leg power. The grip dynamometer tests strength, the ruler drop tests reaction time, and the Illinois test measures agility.

questions.q: In the SPOR principles of training, what does the 'S' stand for?
questions.explain: SPOR stands for Specificity, Progressive overload, Reversibility and Tedium. Specificity means training must match the demands of the sport.

questions.q: What does the 'FITT' principle stand for?
questions.explain: FITT stands for Frequency, Intensity, Time and Type. It is used to apply progressive overload safely to a training programme.

questions.q: A performer stops training for several weeks due to injury and loses fitness. Which principle of training explains this?
questions.explain: Reversibility means that fitness is lost if training stops or intensity drops, often summarised as 'use it or lose it'.

questions.q: Gradually increasing the amount of training so the body is worked harder than normal, but without doing too much too soon, describes which principle?
questions.explain: Progressive overload means gradually making training harder over time so the body adapts and improves, while avoiding injury from overloading too quickly.

questions.q: Which training method involves periods of hard work followed by periods of rest or recovery?
questions.explain: Interval training alternates high-intensity work periods with rest or recovery. HIIT (high-intensity interval training) is an intense form of this.

questions.q: 'Fartlek' training is best described as...
options: 'Speed play' - varying pace and terrain during continuous exercise
Training at one steady pace with no rest
questions.explain: Fartlek is Swedish for 'speed play'. It varies pace and terrain during continuous exercise, developing both aerobic and anaerobic fitness.

questions.q: Which training method is most specific for developing explosive power, e.g. bounding and depth jumps?
questions.explain: Plyometric training uses explosive movements such as bounding, hopping and depth jumps to develop power.

questions.q: A marathon runner wants to improve aerobic endurance with a long steady run. Which method suits this best?
questions.explain: Continuous training is sustained, steady-pace aerobic exercise (e.g. a long run) that develops cardiovascular endurance, ideal for a marathon runner.

questions.q: Which of these is a benefit of a cool-down after exercise?
options: It replaces the need for a warm-up
It raises body temperature ready to perform
It helps remove lactic acid and gradually lowers the heart rate
It reduces the range of movement at joints
questions.explain: A cool-down keeps the heart rate gently elevated to help remove waste products such as lactic acid and reduce muscle soreness, gradually returning the body to rest.

questions.q: Which of these best helps to prevent injury during training?
options: Skipping the warm-up to save energy
Using correct technique and appropriate equipment/clothing
questions.explain: Injury prevention includes warming up, using correct technique, wearing appropriate clothing and protective equipment, and not overloading too quickly.

questions.q: Which formula is used to estimate a person's maximum heart rate?
questions.explain: Maximum heart rate (in beats per minute) is estimated as 220 minus your age.

questions.q: A 15-year-old wants to train in the aerobic zone (60-80% of max HR). Roughly what heart-rate range should they aim for?
questions.explain: Max HR = 220 - 15 = 205 bpm. 60% is about 123 bpm and 80% is about 164 bpm, so the aerobic training zone is roughly 123-164 bpm.
